<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, OpenList is a full-stack, extensible file-listing web application (“alist” fork) with:
  • A SolidJS-based frontend (in public/dist)  
  • A Gin-based Go backend (server/ and internal/)  
  • A plugin-style “drivers” layer for remote storage integrations  
  • A relational metadata store (via internal/db)  
  • Background workers for offline download and tasks  

Here is how to translate this into a clear, accurate system design diagram:

1. Identify Main Components  
   a. Frontend (UI Layer)  
     – public/dist: compiled SolidJS app  
     – Routes to backend via REST/WebSocket  

   b. Backend Web API (Application Layer)  
     – server/: HTTP router, handlers, middlewares  
     – internal/net: HTTP serving utilities  
     – internal/message: HTTP and WS messaging  
     – cmd/: CLI entrypoints (admin, server, storage, user, etc.)  

   c. Core Domain Services (Domain Layer)  
     – internal/authn: authentication & session  
     – internal/conf: configuration loader  
     – internal/db: metadata persistence (users, settings, tasks, storages)  
     – internal/model: request/response and domain models  
     – internal/task: task manager and workers  
     – internal/op & internal/fs: high-level file operations  

   d. Driver/Adapter Layer  
     – drivers/: 60+ storage plugins (S3, GoogleDrive, FTP, WebDAV, etc.)  
     – internal/driver: standardized driver interface  
     – internal/offline_download: adapters for background transfer (aria2, qbit…)  

   e. Database  
     – A SQL store (Postgres/MySQL/SQLite) accessed via internal/db and ORM-like utils  

   f. External Systems  
     – Remote storage services (AWS S3, Google Drive, Baidu Netdisk, etc.)  
     – Optional message brokers or cron (pkg/cron)  
     – Docker or container orchestration (Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml)  

2. Show Relationships & Data-Flow  
   • The Frontend issues API calls (REST/WS) → Backend HTTP Router  
   • Router dispatches to Handlers → Domain Services  
   • Domain Services coordinate:  
     – Authn → user/session validation  
     – Config → load settings  
     – DB → read/write metadata  
     – FS/Op → assemble file/dir structures  
     – Driver → perform remote storage calls  
     – Task Manager → enqueue background jobs  
   • Drivers invoke External Storage APIs  
   • Offline download subsystem schedules and retrieves files, updating DB status  
   • Responses flow back up: Driver → Domain → HTTP → Frontend  

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns  
   – Layered architecture (Presentation → Application → Domain → Infrastructure)  
   – Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters): internal/driver defines ports, drivers/* are adapters  
   – Modular plugin system for storage backends  
   – CLI and server share core libraries (internal/* and pkg/*)  
   – Worker subsystem for asynchronous tasks  

4. Diagramming Guidelines  
   a. Draw separate shapes for:  
      – Frontend (browser)  
      – API Gateway (Gin Server)  
      – Domain Services (authn, fs, op, task)  
      – Driver Interface & Plugins  
      – Database (cylinder icon)  
      – External Storage Services (cloud icons)  
   b. Use directional arrows to show:  
      – HTTP/WS calls (Frontend → API)  
      – Internal calls (API → Domain → Driver/DB)  
      – Asynchronous events (API → Task Queue → Worker → DB/Driver)  
   c. Color-code by layer:  
      – Blue = Presentation (frontend)  
      – Green = Application & Domain (server/ + internal/)  
      – Yellow = Infrastructure Adapters (drivers/, offline_download/)  
      – Orange = External systems (cloud services)  
      – Gray = Database  
   d. Label each arrow with protocol or method (e.g., “REST JSON”, “gRPC?”, “SQL query”, “Plugin call”)  

5. Tailoring to This Project  
   – Emphasize the driver plugin architecture: show “internal/driver” port and multiple driver boxes connecting to diverse external clouds  
   – Show background download scheduler (internal/task + internal/offline_download) as a separate swimlane  
   – Illustrate the shared core libraries (pkg/) as reusable utility blocks invoked by both server and CLI  

6. Must-Include Diagram Elements  
   – Component names matching folder names (e.g., “server/handles”, “drivers/aliyundrive”)  
   – Arrows for data flow and dependencies  
   – Color/shape distinctions for types (UI vs API vs worker vs external)  
   – A legend explaining colors and shapes  

By following these steps, you’ll capture all essential elements—frontend, API, domain services, driver plugins, DB, background workers, and external storages—in a single, coherent architecture diagram that mirrors OpenList’s modular, layered design.  
</explanation>
